task.name: Diagnose flow has no counterpart rule against under-scoping a categorically-stated symptom
task.story_text:
## Problem

The diagnose flow instructs the agent to bound the confirmed cause to the issue's stated symptom and to record anything else as a related finding. That rule exists for a real failure — diagnoses absorbing adjacent problems and over-scoping the fix (#1724). It has no counterpart for the inverse failure: when an issue states its symptom categorically ("every surface", "any story", "regardless of X"), a diagnosis that stops at the first reproducing location silently narrows the fix below what the issue claimed, and nothing downstream notices.

The downstream steps structurally cannot catch it. The dev implements the confirmed cause as the scope. Symptom verification reproduces the originally reported case and confirms it is fixed — which it genuinely is. A diagnosis covering one instance of a categorical symptom passes every check that currently exists.

## Evidence this recurs

- **#1070** — its own title reads "incomplete scope of #156/#290"; body: "Both were closed with claims that exceed what shipped."
- **#1377** — "same failure mode #1375 was supposed to fix". #1375 stated a general rule; the fix enumerated two specific contexts instead. Refiled 40 minutes after close.
- **#969** — #965 claimed coverage "regardless of how many times the sprint resumed"; the fix reached only the completed-read path.
- **#1215** — #1130 offered four directions, one labelled "not requirements"; the fix implemented that one.
- **#1917** — #1364 claimed "every user-facing surface"; the fix reached the DEV-phase payloads alone. Refiled 2.5 months later.

Four of the five refilings explicitly cite the earlier issue, so provenance is usually recovered. The cost is repeated diagnose/fix/review cycles and the erosion of "closed" as a reliable signal — not lost history.

Note on scope of this issue: the diagnose flow is a *prospective* gap. Several of the cases above predate the current diagnose flow or were authored through intake remediation rather than by the diagnose agent, so this is not a retrospective root cause for any single one of them. The gap is real going forward regardless.

## The tension to resolve

Any change here pushes against the existing anti-scope-creep rule, which was added recently for a real failure. Without a stated distinction the two rules oscillate. The line worth testing: a location that is structurally analogous to the confirmed cause — the same construct, the same omission, at a sibling site — is part of the same defect and belongs in scope. A different defect that merely lives nearby remains a related finding.

## Acceptance criteria

- When an issue's stated symptom asserts categorical scope, the diagnosis accounts for structurally analogous locations rather than stopping at the first reproducing one — either covering them in the affected code path or recording which were examined and excluded.
- Diagnoses of issues whose symptom is scoped to a single concrete instance do not broaden as a result of this change.
- The distinction between a structurally analogous location and an adjacent-but-different defect is stated explicitly enough that the two scoping rules do not contradict one another.
- Review and symptom verification distinguish "the reported instance is fixed" from "the symptom's stated scope is covered."

findings.description: A bug whose expected behavior says Any story with notes should preserve them was treated as non-categorical, so a complete diagnosis with no symptom scope coverage had no missing required fields.

A bug that states its symptom categorically but qualifies the quantified noun with a relative clause — 'Any story that fails review is retried.' or 'Every renderer that is registered drops the field.' — is classified as non-categorical, so the scope-coverage requirement does not arm and a diagnosis covering only the first reproducing location can land as fix-ready.

finding_registry.description: A bug whose expected behavior says Any story with notes should preserve them was treated as non-categorical, so a complete diagnosis with no symptom scope coverage had no missing required fields.

A bug that states its symptom categorically but qualifies the quantified noun with a relative clause — 'Any story that fails review is retried.' or 'Every renderer that is registered drops the field.' — is classified as non-categorical, so the scope-coverage requirement does not arm and a diagnosis covering only the first reproducing location can land as fix-ready.

Categorical claims whose scope noun is absent from the curated vocabulary — 'Every phase should emit an audit record.', 'Every worktree should be cleaned up.', 'Every dependency must be resolved before scheduling.' — are classified as non-categorical, so the scope-coverage requirement does not arm and a diagnosis reaching one location can land as fix-ready.

A one-run symptom such as 'Each phase of the run is shown once for run 42' is classified as categorical, so diagnose marks an otherwise complete single-instance diagnosis partial unless it adds scope coverage.

A concrete symptom whose quantifier governs a hint noun that is then narrowed by a trailing prepositional phrase — 'All tasks in this one sprint are duplicated.' — is classified as asserting categorical scope, so a complete diagnosis of that single occurrence is refused as fix-ready and the run reports failure; the same shape already fired for the older hint nouns ('All surfaces in this one command are broken.'), and adding task, agent, phase, dependency and worktree widens how often it can occur.
A bug body whose expected behavior says Every story in every sprint should preserve notes is classified as non-categorical, so diagnose can land a fix-ready artifact without symptom scope coverage.

A categorically stated symptom whose quantified noun is followed by a prepositional phrase naming another scope noun is classified as non-categorical — 'Every path in every run must be logged.', 'Every surface for each run should show the id.', 'Any story in the sprint should be retried.' and 'Every renderer for the sprint should include the branch.' all return non-categorical, so no scope-coverage record is required and a diagnosis reaching one location can land as fix-ready; the same sentences classified categorical before the narrowing suppression was added.

A sentence whose subject is quantified categorically but which ends with a prepositional phrase naming one concrete instance — 'Every surface should include the run id in this run.', 'Every provider must retry on the same path for this command.' — is classified as non-categorical because the suppression now also scans the text after the verb, so no scope-coverage record is required for the categorical subject.

soft: Coordinator is pure Python — no LLM calls for routing or process decisions
Schema validation is the integrity boundary — do not relax cross-validation rules

Keep modules single-purpose. Extract when a responsibility separates from its neighbours — never to satisfy a line count. Putting a change in an already-large module is correct if that is where it belongs; a module carved at whatever line got the count down is worse than the large module it came from.
Keep pure-data types in low-dependency modules with stdlib-only imports
Separate prompt construction, output parsing, and coordinator control flow

When adding or modifying data that flows between coordinator phases, instrument the change so the actual values are visible in the audit trail — diagnosing sprint failures requires tracing real data, not reconstructing it
Do not create files outside src/, tests/, or docs/. If you need a scratch file for exploration, delete it before committing.

Changes that affect coordinator phase boundaries, state handoff between phases, or adaptive routing/config propagation must include seam-level integration tests covering the touched boundary. Unit tests alone are insufficient when correctness depends on cross-phase state flow.
